questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: recognise an identity and count its solutions
questions.stem: A courier prices a parcel as 3 dollars per kilogram plus a 12 dollar handling fee. A clerk rewrites the same price as 3 times the quantity kilograms plus 4, then sets the two versions equal. How many parcel weights make the two versions agree?

options.text: Every weight agrees, since expanding the bracketed form returns the original price
Exactly one weight agrees, since setting two equal prices pins down a number
options.misconception: assumes an equation containing a variable must have a single solution

options.text: No weight agrees, since the bracket changes what the courier is charging
options.misconception: believes introducing a bracket always changes the meaning of a rule

options.text: Two weights agree, since the fee and the per kilogram rate can both be matched
options.misconception: expects two solutions from an equation that reduces to one statement

questions.explanation: Expanding 3 times the quantity x plus 4 gives 3x plus 12, which is the original price term for term, so the equation holds whatever value x takes. An equation that stays true for every value is an identity and has infinitely many solutions. The trap is expecting one answer because a variable is present, but once the bracket is expanded nothing is left to solve for.
questions.hint: Expand the bracketed version and compare it with the unbracketed one term by term.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: identify an equation that simplifies to a false statement
questions.stem: A hire firm charges 5 dollars per hour plus a 3 dollar fee, and a rival charges 5 dollars per hour less a 4 dollar discount. A driver sets the two bills equal for the same number of hours. How many hour counts satisfy that equation?

options.text: No hour count works, since equal rates with different constants never meet
Exactly one hour count works, since the fixed gap can be balanced by more hours
options.misconception: believes a fixed difference between two rules can be repaid by staying longer

options.text: Every hour count works, since both firms charge the same rate per hour
options.misconception: reads matching coefficients as though they also make the constants agree

options.text: Two hour counts work, one below and one above the point where the fees cancel
options.misconception: expects two crossings for a pair of rules with equal rates

questions.explanation: Subtracting 5x from both sides leaves 3 equal to negative 4, which is false, so no value of x can rescue the equation. Two rules sharing a coefficient but carrying different constants draw parallel lines that never intersect, which is the picture behind an empty solution set. The trap is trusting the shared hourly rate and concluding the bills agree somewhere; the constants alone decide it.
questions.hint: Cancel the terms that contain the variable and read off the number statement that is left.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a linear equation with a fixed fee
questions.learningObjective: solve a one unknown linear equation that hides a fixed fee
questions.stem: A laundry bills a 6 dollar cleaning charge plus 2 dollars per bag, and one order came to 38 dollars. How many bags were washed? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Subtract the cleaning charge first to get 2b equal to 32, then divide by 2 to find b equal to 16 bags. Working backwards confirms it, since 2 times 16 is 32 and the cleaning charge brings the order to 38. Subtracting the charge from only one side, or dividing 38 by 2 before moving it, is what produces a wrong count.
questions.hint: Move the fixed charge across first, then divide by the per bag rate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Solving a linear equation with variable on both sides
questions.learningObjective: collect the variable terms before isolating the unknown
questions.stem: A winch rule says pulling force equals 5 times the drum turns minus 4 newtons, and a load needs 36 newtons. How many turns are required? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Add 4 to both sides so that 5t equal to 40, then divide by 5 to get 8 turns. The check is immediate, since 5 times 8 is 40 and removing the 4 leaves a force of exactly 36. Adding before dividing matters, because dividing 36 by 5 and then adjusting gives a turn count that does not reproduce the force.
questions.hint: Undo the subtraction before undoing the multiplication.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Parallel rules with no shared point
questions.learningObjective: explain why equal rates with different constants give no shared point
questions.stem: On one map, trail A climbs 2 metres for every metre across and starts 6 metres up, while trail B climbs at the same 2 to 1 rate but starts 1 metre up. A walker wants a point that lies on both trail descriptions. What is the outcome?

options.text: No such point exists, since equal rates with different starting heights never meet
Exactly one point exists, since equal steepness fixes where the trails cross
options.misconception: believes two rules with the same slope must still intersect somewhere

options.text: Every point of one trail is on the other, since the two rates agree
options.misconception: confuses a shared slope with a single shared line

options.text: The point exists only where the trails touch the horizontal axis of the map
options.misconception: believes an intersection must lie on a coordinate axis

questions.explanation: Rules with the same coefficient but different constants are parallel lines, so the gap between them never closes and no point can satisfy both. Setting the rules equal cancels the variable and leaves a false statement, which is the algebraic form of the same fact. The trap is assuming matching steepness must produce a crossing; only different steepness guarantees one.
questions.hint: Compare the rates of change first, then compare the starting heights.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Distribution error that invents a contradiction
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a misdistribution that turns an identity into a contradiction
questions.stem: A student is told that a price rule is 4 dollars per item plus a 12 dollar fee, and that the same rule was written as 4 times the quantity items plus 3. She cancels the 4x terms, writes 12 equal to 3, and declares the rule impossible. Where does her work break down?

options.text: She did not multiply the outside 4 by the 3 inside the bracket, which gives 4x plus 12
She multiplied correctly, so the rule really is contradictory and her answer stands
options.misconception: accepts an incomplete distribution as valid algebra

options.text: She should have divided both sides by 4 before comparing the two versions
options.misconception: suggests division as a fix for a distribution that was never done

options.text: She should have moved the 12 to the right rather than cancelling the 4x terms
options.misconception: believes moving a constant repairs a bracket left undistributed

questions.explanation: A factor outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it, so 4 times the quantity x plus 3 is 4x plus 12, not 4x plus 3. With that correction both sides are the same rule and the equation holds for every number of items. The trap is reading the leftover false statement 12 equal to 3 as a property of the problem, when it is a symptom of the misdistribution.
questions.hint: Ask what the 4 outside the bracket still has to multiply.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: classify solution sets from the statement left after simplification
questions.stem: A solver outputs one row per equation. After collecting terms the first leaves 0 equal to 0, the second leaves 0 equal to 9, the third leaves x equal to 5, and the fourth leaves 4 equal to 4. Which statement about the solution sets is correct?

options.text: The first and fourth equations have infinitely many solutions between them
Only the third equation has a single value that satisfies it exactly
options.misconception: misses that the remainder x equal to 5 is also the single solution case

options.text: The second equation is the one with infinitely many solutions listed
options.misconception: reads a false remainder as a true one when counting solutions

options.text: None of the four equations has a solution at all, since the variable is gone
options.misconception: treats a vanished variable as proof that no value can satisfy the row

questions.explanation: A remainder such as 0 equal to 0 or 4 equal to 4 is a true statement that no longer mentions the variable, so it holds for every value and those two equations have infinitely many solutions. A false remainder such as 0 equal to 9 rules every value out and gives an empty set. A remainder that still contains the variable, like x equal to 5, names exactly one solution.
questions.hint: Look at whether the leftover statement still mentions the variable, and whether it is true.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: recognise an identity and count its solutions
questions.stem: A farm inspects four equations that appear along a water-pipe schedule. Which one has infinitely many solutions rather than exactly one or none?

options.text: 5 times the quantity t plus 1 equal to 5t plus 1
5 times the quantity t plus 1 equal to 5t plus 3
options.misconception: notices the coefficient of t matches and assumes both sides are the same expression

options.text: 5 times the quantity t plus 1 equal to 5t, the left side lacks a final term
options.misconception: treats a missing constant as evidence of many solutions rather than a false statement

options.text: 5 times the quantity t plus 1 equal to 4t plus 1
options.misconception: reads a differing coefficient of t as if it implied infinitely many values

questions.explanation: Distributing the 5 turns the correct option into 5t plus 1, which is exactly its right side, so it is an identity with infinitely many solutions. The option with 5t plus 3 also has equal coefficients of t, but the constants differ, so the simplified remainder is a false statement and the equation has no solution. Missing or differing constants and differing coefficients both produce a single unique solution when the terms still balance.
questions.hint: Expand each left side first, then compare the constant on each side before counting solutions.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: decide when an equation has an empty solution set
questions.stem: A robotics club tunes two track layouts with the equations y equals 4x plus 3 and y equals 4x minus 9 for the same pair of tracks. How many points of overlap do the two layouts have?

options.text: None, because equal slopes with different intercepts describe parallel tracks
Exactly one, because solving the pair always isolates a single value of x
options.misconception: assumes every two-equation pair must cross once when the coefficients of x match

options.text: Infinitely many, because the tracks share the same rate of change in y
options.misconception: reads a shared slope as a guarantee of a shared track rather than a shared direction

options.text: Exactly two, one where each track crosses the horizontal axis
options.misconception: counts axis crossings of separate lines as points shared by both tracks

questions.explanation: Setting the two rules equal cancels x and leaves 3 equal to negative 9, which is false, so the system has an empty solution set. Both graphs share the slope 4 but sit 12 units apart vertically, so they are parallel and never meet. A system with equal slopes is an identity only when the intercepts also match, and here they do not.
questions.hint: Set the two right-hand sides equal and see which constant statement survives.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: identify a system whose equations describe the same line
questions.stem: A surveyor records one boundary as 3x minus 6y equal to 12. Which second boundary produces infinitely many common points with the first one?

options.text: 6x minus 12y equal to 24, which is the first boundary scaled by a factor of 2
6x minus 12y equal to 18, which keeps the same coefficient ratio but a different constant
options.misconception: matches the coefficients and ignores that the constant must scale by the same factor

options.text: 6x minus 6y equal to 24, which doubles only the coefficient of the first variable
options.misconception: scales one coefficient and expects the whole line to be unchanged

options.text: 3x minus 6y equal to 24, which keeps the left side and raises the constant only
options.misconception: believes shifting the constant still leaves the same set of points

questions.explanation: When one equation is a nonzero multiple of the other, both describe the same line, so every point on that line satisfies both equations and the solution set is infinite. Doubling the whole equation moves the constant to 24, so the pair is two copies of one boundary rather than two different ones. Any option that scales the coefficients but not the constant gives parallel lines instead, with no common point at all.
questions.hint: Check whether the second equation is a whole multiple of the first, constant included.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Graph of a linear equation in two variables
questions.learningObjective: compute the value of a linear rule at a stated input
questions.stem: A drainage pipe follows the rule y equals 3x minus 5. What is the value of y at the input x equals 4? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Substituting 4 for x gives 3 times 4 minus 5, which is 12 minus 5, so the output is 7. The order matters: multiplying before subtracting avoids the common slip of computing 4 minus 5 first, which would give a negative 3. Plotting the point 4 and 7 on the graph of the rule confirms that it lies on the line.
questions.hint: Multiply the input by 3 first, then subtract 5 from the product.

questions.topic: Graph of a linear equation in two variables

questions.stem: A mechanic's charge follows the rule y equals 6x plus 20 for x hours of work. A customer was billed 92 dollars. For how many hours was the work logged? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Subtracting 20 from 92 leaves 72, and dividing by the hourly rate 6 gives 12 hours. Checking forward confirms it, because 6 times 12 plus 20 is 92, so the hours reproduce the bill exactly. Dividing 92 by 6 before subtracting the fixed charge gives a smaller value and is the usual mistake.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: find the horizontal-axis crossing of a linear rule
questions.stem: A wire is modelled by y equals 2x plus 8. At what value of x does the wire cross the horizontal axis? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A crossing of the horizontal axis happens where the output is zero, so solve 2x plus 8 equal to zero by subtracting 8 and then dividing by 2, which gives x equal to negative 4. Substituting negative 4 back gives 2 times negative 4 plus 8, which is zero, so the point really is on the axis. Dropping the sign of 8 when it moves across the equals sign is what turns this into positive 4.
questions.hint: Set y to zero and solve for x, watching the sign as the 8 crosses over.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Slope from an equation in standard form
questions.learningObjective: read the slope out of a standard-form equation by isolating y
questions.stem: A pipeline is described by 6x minus 3y equal to 15. When the equation is rearranged into the form y equals a multiple of x plus a constant, what is that multiple? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Move 6x across to get negative 3y equal to negative 6x plus 15, then divide every term by negative 3 to obtain y equal to 2x minus 5, so the multiple is 2. Both negatives must travel together through the division, since a single division by negative 3 applied to only part of the line would leave an unbalanced equation. Checking with a point confirms the slope: the pair 0 and negative 5 and the pair 3 and 1 both sit on the line.
questions.hint: Isolate y, then divide every term by the coefficient of y and keep the sign straight.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: apply the equal-slope condition for two lines to be parallel
questions.stem: Two detour routes are written as 7x minus 2y equal to 14 and 7x minus 2y equal to 3. Which relationship do the two routes have?

options.text: They are parallel and distinct, since the slope matches and the constants differ
They meet exactly once, since the two routes are written with different numbers
options.misconception: assumes different right-hand constants guarantee a crossing for any two lines

options.text: They are the same route, since the left-hand sides are identical expressions
options.misconception: ignores the constant terms when deciding whether two equations coincide

options.text: They are perpendicular, since subtracting one equation from the other gives zero
options.misconception: believes cancelling identical left sides proves a right angle between the lines

questions.explanation: Two equations with the same left side and different right sides have the same slope but different intercepts, so their graphs are parallel lines that never intersect. Slackening nothing else changes that conclusion, because the slope is decided by the ratio of the two coefficients of the variables, not by the constant. Perpendicularity would need the slopes to be negative reciprocals of one another.
questions.hint: Compare the coefficients of the variables first, then compare the constant terms.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: find the slope of a line perpendicular to a line of given slope
questions.stem: A valley floor runs along the line y equals 3x minus 2, and a fault line crosses it at a right angle. Which of these claims about the fault line is sound?
A valley floor follows the rule y equals 3x minus 2, and a fault line crosses it at a right angle. What is the slope of the fault line? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals, so the slope 3 becomes negative one third, and the product 3 times negative one third equals negative 1, which is the test for a right angle. Reporting negative 3 keeps the steepness and merely flips the direction, while positive one third rises like the valley floor, so neither can form a right angle with it.
questions.hint: Take the negative reciprocal of the slope 3, so the two slopes multiply to negative 1.
Multiply the two slopes and see which option gives exactly negative 1.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a vertical line has an undefined slope
questions.stem: A survey beam runs along the graph of x equals negative 7. What is the slope of that beam, and which reasoning supports the answer?

options.text: It is undefined, because the run is zero for any two points on the beam
It is zero, because the beam never changes its horizontal position
options.misconception: confuses an unchanging input with an unchanging output and reads a slope of zero

options.text: It is one, because every unit climbed covers one unit of horizontal travel
options.misconception: assumes a unit of horizontal travel exists when the line has no horizontal change

options.text: It is negative 7, the number that appears on the right side of the equation
options.misconception: reads the constant in the equation as though it were a slope value

questions.explanation: Slope is rise divided by run, and on a vertical line the run is zero for every pair of points, so the quotient is undefined rather than any finite number. A slope of zero belongs to a horizontal line instead, where the rise is zero and the run is not. No vertical line has a numeric slope, which is also why the equations of vertical lines are written with x alone and carry no value for a multiple of x.
questions.hint: Draw two points on the beam and measure the change in the first coordinate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a vertical line from a line of zero slope
questions.stem: A crane track is described by y equals 5 and a guide rail by x equals 5. What is the difference in slope between the two, and why?

options.text: The track has slope zero while the rail has no defined slope, since their runs differ
Both have slope zero, since neither equation contains a term multiplying a variable
options.misconception: reads a skipped variable as a zero slope for both the horizontal and vertical cases

options.text: Both have undefined slope, since neither equation can be solved for two variables
options.misconception: believes a slope only exists when an equation can be solved for an expression in two variables

options.text: The track has slope 5 while the rail has slope 5, since both equal the same number
options.misconception: reads the shared constant on the right as a slope for both descriptions

questions.explanation: The equation y equals 5 has a zero numerator because y never changes, so its slope is zero, while x equals 5 has a zero denominator because x never changes, so its slope is undefined. The two equations look similar in shape but describe perpendicular lines: one horizontal and one vertical. Reporting zero for both is the standard slip, because it applies the horizontal case to a vertical line.
questions.hint: For each line, decide whether the change in the first coordinate or the change in the second is zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: compute a slope from two points and use it to classify a line
questions.stem: Two stakes on a roof beam sit at the points where x is 3 and y is 4, and where x is 8 and y is 10. What is the slope of the beam? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The slope is the change in the second coordinate divided by the change in the first, so 10 minus 4 is 6 and 8 minus 3 is 5, giving 6 over 5 which is 1.2. Both differences must be taken in the same order, since reversing only one of them flips the sign of the answer. A third point on the line, such as the pair 13 and 16, sits 5 along and 6 up again, confirming the value.
questions.hint: Subtract the second coordinates over the subtraction of the first coordinates, keeping the order fixed.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Interpreting a solution of a system
questions.learningObjective: read the meaning of a solution pair for two rules in context
questions.stem: A maker sells candles under the rules C equals 8 plus 2n and C equals 3 plus 3n, where n counts candles. A student solves the system, finds n equals 5, and reports that the two rules agree at 5 candles and 18 dollars. Where could that report still be wrong?

options.text: The second equation gives 18 dollars at 5 candles only after checking, since 3 plus 15 is 18
The n value 5 must be divided by 2 first, since the second rule has a coefficient of 3
options.misconception: rescale a solved variable to match a coefficient instead of substituting it back

options.text: The solution must be 5 dollars and 18 candles, since the rules give cost after quantity
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the two quantities when writing the solution pair

options.text: The pair is correct without checking, since one equation is enough to verify the value of n
options.misconception: believes satisfying a single equation of a system is enough to be a solution

questions.explanation: A solution of a system must satisfy every equation at once, so the reported pair has to be tested in both rules: the first gives 8 plus 10 which is 18, and the second gives 3 plus 15 which is also 18. The n value 5 does satisfy both, so the pair is sound, but the reasoning matters because only a joint check rules out a value that was solved from one equation alone. Reporting the pair in the wrong order, or rescaling the solved value, both lose the link between the equations.
questions.hint: Substitute the pair into both equations and confirm that each one balances.

questions.learningObjective: solve a system of two linear equations by substitution

questions.learningObjective: solve a system of two linear equations by elimination
questions.stem: Two tank readings satisfy 2x plus 4y equal to 20 and 4x minus 4y equal to 4. Adding the two equations, what is the value of y? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Adding cancels the y terms and leaves 6x equal to 24, so x equal to 4. Substituting back into the first equation gives 8 plus 4y equal to 20, so 4y equals 12 and y equals 3, and the second equation checks as 16 minus 12 equal to 4. Treating the sum of the two right-hand sides, 24, as the value of x rather than as 6x is the trap, and so is stopping once x is found.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: read a graph change of direction from a table of values
questions.stem: A station logs fuel against distance for a van. The recorded pairs of kilometres and litres are 0 and 40, 50 and 33, 100 and 26, and 150 and 19. Which claim about the graph of these readings is sound?

options.text: It is a straight line of slope negative 0.14 litres per kilometre, since the drop is level
It is a straight line of slope negative 1.4 litres per kilometre, since the drop is level
options.misconception: divides the fuel change by the distance change in the wrong order, inflating the rate

options.text: It is a curve, since the fuel figure falls below zero once the distance grows further
options.misconception: believes the graph must bend as soon as its output would eventually go negative

options.text: It is a straight line of slope zero, since the fuel falls by a fixed amount each time
options.misconception: confuses a constant change in the output with a slope of zero

questions.explanation: Each 50 kilometres removes 7 litres, so the rate is negative 7 over 50, which is negative 0.14 litres per kilometre, and a constant rate of change is exactly what a straight line means. The reading never bends within the listed range, and the fact that the rule would eventually reach zero is a property of the line rather than a curve. A slope of zero would mean the fuel did not change at all.
questions.hint: Divide the change in litres by the change in kilometres between two of the listed pairs.

questions.learningObjective: use a table of pairings to test whether a rule is linear
questions.stem: A pond covers an area logged at the points where the week is 0 and the area is 120, at week 2 and 96, at week 5 and 75, and at week 9 and 45 hectares. Which statement about the graph of these readings is correct?

A straight line fits with slope 5 hectares per week, since the area always falls by more
options.misconception: reports the size of the drop as a positive rate, losing the sign of the decline

options.text: A curve fits, since the area is falling and all shrinking measurements follow a curve
options.misconception: believes any quantity that decreases must trace a curve rather than a line

options.text: A straight line fits with a changing slope, since the weeks are spaced unevenly
options.misconception: mistakes an even spacing of readings for a requirement that rates of change be equal

The slope measured over any pair that does fit, such as 0 and 5, works out to 9 hectares per week. The claim that every falling quantity must curve is wrong, because a constant decrease is precisely a straight line with a negative slope.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: test two standard-form equations for parallelism by comparing coefficient ratios
questions.stem: A park bench plan gives two rails as 2x plus 6y equal to 18 and x plus 3y equal to 11. Which statement about the rails is correct?
A park bench plan gives two rails as 2x plus 6y equals 18 and x plus 3y equals 11. Rewritten with y isolated, what is the slope of the second rail? Report the number only.

The first rail, divided by 2, gives x plus 3y equals 9, which has the same left side and a different constant, so the two rails are parallel rather than coincident. Doubling only the constant of the second rail, or comparing it against the first without scaling, are the two ways this comparison goes wrong.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Perpendicular line through a given point
questions.learningObjective: build the line through a point with the slope perpendicular to a given line
questions.stem: A cable runs along y equals 4x minus 3, and a brace must cross it at a right angle at the point where x is 2 and y is 5. Which equation describes the brace?
A cable runs along y equals 4x minus 3, and a brace must cross it at a right angle at the point where x is 2 and y is 5. What is the slope of the brace? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The brace must have the negative reciprocal of 4, which is negative one quarter, so that the product of the slopes 4 times negative one quarter equals negative 1. The sign and the reciprocal have to be applied together, since negative 4 reverses the direction without changing the steepness, and 4 describes a parallel brace rather than a perpendicular one. A right angle between two non-vertical lines is exactly the product-minus-one condition.
questions.hint: The two slopes must multiply to negative 1, so take the negative reciprocal of 4.
Take the negative reciprocal of the given slope, then use the given point to fix the constant.

questions.topic: Solving a linear equation with fractions
questions.learningObjective: solve an equation containing fractional coefficients exactly
questions.stem: A recipe rule reads two thirds of x equal to 12 when scaled up. What is the value of x? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Multiplying both sides by 3 clears the denominator to give 2x equal to 36, and dividing by 2 gives x equal to 18. Checking, two thirds of 18 is 12, so the original rule balances. Multiplying only the right side, or dividing by two thirds instead of multiplying, is what leads to the common wrong values of 8 or 27.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Misreading an identity as a single solution
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a learner who assumes a variable must resolve to one number
questions.stem: A student simplifies 2 times the quantity x plus 3 equal to 2x plus 6, sees that the x terms cancel, and writes that the answer is x equal to 0. Which statement about the student's work is sound?

options.text: The cancellation leaves 0 equal to 0, which is true for every value, so the solution set is infinite
The cancellation is fine but the answer should be x equal to 6, since the constant survives
options.misconception: keeps a constant that has already been matched on the other side as if it were isolated

options.text: The student should solve 2x equal to 6 instead, which gives the unique answer of 3
options.misconception: drops the bracket and treats the equation as a two-term one rather than an identity

options.text: Because the x terms cancel the equation has no solution, so the answer x equal to 0 is unsupported
options.misconception: treats a cancelled variable as proof that no value can satisfy the equation

questions.explanation: Expanding the bracket gives 2x plus 6 on the left, exactly the right side, so the equation holds for every value of x and has infinitely many solutions. The cancelled variable leaves the true statement 0 equal to 0, which is the algebraic marker of an identity rather than the loss of all solutions. Reporting x equal to 0 invents a constraint the equation never placed.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket fully, then read what the cancelled statement actually says.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Testing which equation is an identity
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claimed solution count by substituting a test value
questions.stem: A drum tone equation reads 6 minus x equal to the quantity x plus 6, all multiplied by negative 1, per the workshop notes. Which test shows the claim that it has no solution is false?

options.text: Substituting x equal to 0 makes both sides equal 6, so one solution exists already
Substituting x equal to 6 makes both sides zero, which proves infinitely many solutions
options.misconception: treats a single success at one chosen value as proof that every value works

options.text: Cancelling the x terms leaves 6 equal to negative 6, so no value can ever work
options.misconception: ignores that the bracket on the right reverses the sign of its terms when expanded

options.text: Dividing both sides by negative 1 removes the variable, so the equation cannot be solved
options.misconception: believes scaling an equation by negative 1 deletes the variable

questions.explanation: Expanding the right side gives negative x minus 6, so the equation reads 6 minus x equal to negative x minus 6, and the x terms cancel to leave 6 equal to negative 6, which is false. The claim of no solution is therefore true, but option A reports a value at which both sides are 6, which contradicts that expansion and so exposes the test as invalid. Because a linear equation with the same coefficient of x on both sides and different constants has no solution, the sound test must find a contradiction rather than a coincidence.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket on the right before comparing the two sides.

questions.stem: A battery charge is graphed from the points where minutes are 0 and percent is 100, and minutes are 20 and percent is 70. What does the graph give for the charge at 50 minutes? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The line falls 30 percent over 20 minutes, which is 1.5 percent per minute, so at 50 minutes the charge is 100 minus 1.5 times 50, which is 25 percent. A negative reading only tells us the battery is flat long before then, and the linear rule still produces such a number if the model is pushed past where it applies. Assuming the charge cannot fall below zero and answering zero instead is a good modelling instinct but it is not what the graph says.

questions.learningObjective: connect a slope of zero to a horizontal graph
questions.stem: A pipeline runs level along the line y equals 9 metres. What is the slope of that pipeline? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A level line never changes its output, so the rise is zero while the run is not, and zero divided by any nonzero number is zero. This is the opposite of a vertical line, where the run is zero and the slope is undefined. Treating a level line as having no slope at all, or as having an undefined one, mixes up which coordinate is failing to change.

questions.topic: Slope as a rate of change
questions.learningObjective: read a slope as a rate of change with its units
questions.stem: A tank fills at 6 litres every 5 minutes, and the level is graphed against time. What is the rate of rise in litres per minute? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The slope is the change in level divided by the change in time, so 6 litres over 5 minutes equals 1.2 litres per minute. Writing the ratio the other way round, 5 over 6, gives minutes per litre, which answers a different question. The units are part of the value, since a slope without its units cannot be checked against the situation.

questions.stem: A delivery cost graph crosses the vertical axis at 12 dollars and falls by 0.5 dollars for every kilometre. Which rule matches that graph?
A delivery cost graph crosses the vertical axis at 12 dollars and falls by 0.5 dollars for every kilometre. How much does the graph charge for a distance of 6 kilometres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rule is the vertical intercept 12 plus the slope negative 0.5 times the distance, and at 6 kilometres that is 12 minus 3, which is 9 dollars. Taking the fall in the wrong direction would give 15, putting the intercept below the axis would give 6, and swapping the rate with the intercept would give 3. A falling line still starts at its vertical intercept, and the rate decides how quickly it leaves that starting value.

questions.topic: Graphs of two equations in one variable
questions.learningObjective: interpret the solution of a one variable equation as an intersection on a graph
questions.stem: A learner graphs y equal to 2x plus 3 and y equal to 5 on the same axes to solve 2x plus 3 equal to 5, then reads the answer off the drawing. Which statement about that method is correct?

options.text: The solution is the first coordinate of the crossing point, which is 1
The solution is the second coordinate of the crossing point, which is 5
options.misconception: reads the height of the crossing as the solution of the one variable equation

options.text: The solution is where each line crosses the horizontal axis, which is negative 1.5
options.misconception: solves each equation against zero instead of against each other

options.text: The solution does not exist, because one of the equations has no x term at all
options.misconception: believes a graph with a missing variable cannot intersect a line

questions.explanation: Graphing each side of a one variable equation turns the problem into a pair of lines, and the value that satisfies the equation is the first coordinate where the two lines meet. Here 2x plus 3 equal to 5 gives x equal to 1, and the crossing point on the graph is 1 and 5, so the first coordinate is the answer. Reading the second coordinate gives the right side of the equation rather than the value of the variable.
questions.hint: Find where the two graphs meet, then report the first coordinate of that point.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: translate two purchase conditions into a system and solve it
questions.stem: A shop sells pens at p dollars each and notebooks at n dollars each. Two pens with three notebooks cost 19 dollars, and three pens with one notebook cost 18 dollars. What is the value of p? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: From the second equation n equals 18 minus 3p, and substituting into the first gives 2p plus 3 times the quantity 18 minus 3p equal to 19, so negative 7p equals negative 35 and p equals 5. Then n equals 3, and both statements check: 10 plus 9 is 19, and 15 plus 3 is 18, which is the check that confirms the system. Attaching each cost to the wrong statement, or forgetting to distribute the 3, are the usual sources of a wrong pair.
questions.hint: Isolate n from one equation and substitute it into the other before solving for p.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: spot the value that makes a parameterised system unsolvable
questions.stem: A system reads kx minus 2y equal to 6 and 3x minus 2y equal to 5. How many whole number values of k from 0 to 6 give this system exactly one solution? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Subtracting the second equation from the first gives the quantity k minus 3 times x equal to 1, which has a unique solution exactly when k minus 3 is not zero. That excludes only k equal to 3, so six of the seven whole numbers from 0 to 6 remain: 0, 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6. Counting all seven, or counting the excluded value as a solution, are the two slips this item is aimed at.

questions.learningObjective: solve a system where one equation already isolates a variable
questions.stem: A fuel budget gives the rule x minus y equals 5 together with the rule x plus 2y equals 20. What is the value of y? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: From the first equation x equals y plus 5, and substituting into the second gives 3y plus 5 equal to 20, so 3y equals 15 and y equals 5. Then x equals 10, and both equations check: 10 minus 5 is 5, and 10 plus 10 is 20. Substituting y plus 5 into the wrong equation, or adding the two equations without collecting terms, are the slips that give a different value.

questions.stem: Two balances read 2x plus 5y equal to 26 and 3x minus 5y equal to 11. Adding the two equations, what is the value of x? Report the number only.

Substituting back into the first equation gives 5y equal to 26 minus 14.8, which is 11.2, so y equals 2.24, and both equations balance. Treating the sum of the right-hand sides, 37, as the value of x instead of 5x is the trap here.
questions.hint: Add first to remove y, then divide by the coefficient of x.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: choose the method that fits the shape of a given system
questions.stem: A builder is handed the system 3x plus 4y equal to 24 together with y equal to 2x minus 6. Which statement about choosing a solving method is sound?

options.text: Substitution suits it, because one equation already states y in terms of x
Elimination is forced, since substitution needs both equations solved for the same variable
options.misconception: believes substitution requires both equations to be arranged in the same form

options.text: Neither method works, because the coefficients 3 and 4 cannot be made to match
options.misconception: ignores that scaling one equation can always bring a coefficient into agreement

options.text: Only graphing works, since a written system with a bracket-less form needs a drawing
options.misconception: believes a graph is required whenever one equation is written in a different form

questions.explanation: Substitution is shortest when an equation already gives one variable in terms of the other, so replacing y with 2x minus 6 produces a single equation in x. Elimination is also possible after rearranging, so the second equation does not force any particular route, and the coefficients 3 and 4 can always be brought to agree by scaling. Choosing the method is about efficiency rather than permission, and both routes reach the same pair.
questions.hint: Look at what each equation gives for free before choosing a method.

questions.learningObjective: read a system in context and reject an impossible reported answer
questions.stem: A model of seats on a shuttle is built for passenger counts up to 40, but a supervisor runs it at 55 and reads negative 3 seats needed. Which conclusion about that reading is sound?

options.text: The model has been pushed past its range, because a seat count cannot go negative
The shuttle truly needs negative 3 seats, so 3 seats should be sold to other shuttles
options.misconception: accepts an output that describes an impossible quantity as a real instruction

options.text: The model is fine, because a negative reading simply means spare seats are available
options.misconception: reinterprets the meaning of the output to rescue a model used outside its range

options.text: The reading should be corrected by adding 55 to it, giving 52 seats as the answer
options.misconception: patches a broken output with arithmetic instead of questioning its range

questions.explanation: A negative number of seats cannot exist, so the output itself is the evidence that the input sits outside the region the model describes. Selling or reinterpreting the negative value keeps using a model that has already disqualified itself. The useful habit is to check the kind and sign of a result against the situation before checking the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask whether a count of that kind can exist before asking whether the arithmetic was right.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: compare two linear graphs by their slopes and intercepts
questions.stem: A broker graphs two plans. Plan A starts at 15 dollars and gains 6 dollars every month, while Plan B starts at 9 dollars and gains 6 dollars every month. What do the graphs show about the plans?

options.text: Two parallel lines 6 dollars apart, because the monthly gain is the same for both
Two lines that cross, because Plan B starts lower so it must catch up with Plan A
options.misconception: believes a lower starting point always produces a crossing when the rates agree

options.text: A single line, because both plans gain the same amount each month
options.misconception: confuses equal slopes with one shared line and forgets the different starting values

options.text: Two lines that grow further apart, because Plan A earns 6 dollars more every month
options.misconception: compares the starting gap as though it were added to the monthly gain

questions.explanation: Both plans have the same slope of 6 dollars per month, so they rise in parallel, and the starting values differ by 6 dollars, which is the fixed vertical gap between them. Because the gap never changes, the two graphs never meet and Plan A stays 6 dollars ahead. A crossing needs different slopes, so the belief that a lower start guarantees a catch-up is false here.
questions.hint: Compare the monthly gains first; equal gains mean parallel lines.

questions.topic: Equation with no solution in standard form
questions.learningObjective: recognise a standard-form equation with an empty solution set
questions.stem: A booking sheet carries the line 2 times the quantity x minus 5 equal to 2x plus 1. What happens when a clerk tries to solve it for x?

options.text: The x terms cancel to a false statement, so no value of x can be booked
The x terms cancel to a true statement, so every booking is possible
options.misconception: assumes cancellation of the variable always leaves a statement that holds for every value

options.text: The x terms survive on one side, so exactly one booking value is found
options.misconception: expects a variable to remain whenever an equation contains a bracket

options.text: The equation must be divided by 2 first, which removes the contradiction entirely
options.misconception: believes scaling an equation can remove a contradiction left by unequal constants

questions.explanation: Expanding the bracket gives 2x minus 10 on the left, and cancelling the 2x terms leaves negative 10 equal to 1, which is false, so the solution set is empty. No amount of scaling or rearranging can turn a false statement into a solvable one, because every allowed operation preserves truth. This is the same algebra as two parallel lines that never meet.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket and see which statement is left before the x terms cancel.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Identity equation after clearing a fraction
questions.learningObjective: solve a fractional equation that turns out to be an identity
questions.stem: A learner is given the equation x over 4 plus 3 equal to the quantity x plus 12 over 4. The learner multiplies both sides by 4, gets x plus 12 equal to x plus 12, and then writes that there is only one solution. What is the error?

options.text: Both sides became the same expression, which means every value of x is a solution
The learner should have multiplied only the left side by 4, which would leave one solution
options.misconception: believes an operation applied to just one side preserves the solution set

options.text: The learner should have divided both sides by 4 next, giving x equal to x as the answer
options.misconception: treats an identity as a step toward isolating a single value of the variable

options.text: The equation really does have one solution, since multiplying both sides cannot change it
options.misconception: assumes a legitimate operation imposes a single solution on any equation

questions.explanation: Clearing the multiplier 4 makes the two sides identical, x plus 12 on each, so the statement holds for every value of x and the solution set is all real numbers. Multiplying both sides by the same nonzero number never removes or adds solutions, so it cannot be the source of the infinite set. Writing an isolated value as the answer is the error, because nothing is left to isolate.
questions.hint: After clearing the fraction, ask whether the two sides are still the same expression.

A service road runs parallel to the route given by y equals negative 2x plus 7 and passes through the point where x is 3 and y is 1. What is the vertical intercept of the service road? Report the number only.

questions.stem: A conveyor belt rises along the rule y equals 5 plus negative 0.8 times x. What is the slope of the belt? Report the number only.

Reading the 5 as the slope confuses the vertical intercept with the rate of change. Checking with two points on the belt, for example 0 and 5 and 10 and negative 3, gives a change of negative 8 over 10, which is negative 0.8.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: verify a reported solution pair satisfies both equations of a system
questions.stem: A grader is told that the pair x equal to 2 and y equal to 5 solves the system x plus y equal to 7 and 3x plus 2y equal to 16. What single check settles whether the pair is a solution?

options.text: Substitute the pair into both equations and confirm that each one balances
Substitute into either one equation, since a solution of one equation is a solution of the system
options.misconception: treats a single agreement as enough to certify a solution of the whole system

options.text: Add the two equations and check that the pair satisfies the resulting equation
options.misconception: believes an equation formed from the two must be satisfied by the same pair

options.text: Graph one of the equations, since only its line needs to pass through the pair
options.misconception: checks membership on one line and ignores the second line of the system

questions.explanation: A solution of a system has to satisfy every equation in it, so the pair must be substituted into both and each must balance; here 2 plus 5 is 7 and 6 plus 10 is 16, so the pair is genuine. Satisfying the combined equation that results from adding is not enough, because that new equation can be true for pairs that fail one of the originals. The joint check is the only test that certifies a solution.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a tautology makes an equation hold for every value
questions.stem: A textbook claims that an equation which reduces to the statement 0 equal to 0 has no solution. Which statement explains the error in that claim?

options.text: The statement 0 equal to 0 is true for every value of the variable, so the solution set is infinite
The statement 0 equal to 0 is false because zero divided by undefined has no meaning
options.misconception: invents a division that never appears in the reduced equation

options.text: The equation reduces to no variables, so it must be treated as an unsolvable formless line
options.misconception: believes losing all variables automatically empties the solution set

options.text: The claim is right, since an equation with nothing left to solve cannot have solutions
options.misconception: equates the absence of a variable with the absence of solutions

questions.explanation: When every variable cancels and the remaining statement is true, nothing restricts the original variable, so all of its allowed values satisfy the equation. The reduced statement is a property of the equation, not of any particular value, and a true property cannot rule anything out. questions.learningObjective: classify a system from its graphs
questions.stem: A plotting tool draws two lines for a system and reports that the two lines are drawn on top of one another rather than side by side. What follows about the system?

options.text: It is dependent, with every point of the single shared line as a solution
It is inconsistent, because the two equations cannot be told apart when drawn together
options.misconception: mistakes coincident lines for a pair that does not meet

options.text: It has exactly one solution, at the point where the two lines appear to touch
options.misconception: believes two overlapping lines must still meet at a single point

options.text: It is independent, because each equation contributes its own line to the drawing
options.misconception: assumes having two equations always produces two distinct lines

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a word problem stated with two unknown totals
questions.stem: Two crates hold 9 kilograms of apples between them. The heavier crate holds 3 kilograms more than twice the lighter one. How many kilograms does the lighter crate hold? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Let l be the lighter crate. The heavier is 2l plus 3, and the total gives l plus 2l plus 3 equal to 9, so 3l equals 6 and l equals 2 kilograms. The heavier crate then holds 7, and 2 plus 7 equals 9 as stated. Writing the heavier crate as 2 times the quantity l plus 3 adds 3 to the wrong side of the multiplication, which gives a non-integer answer of 2.5.
questions.hint: Twice the lighter amount plus 3 gives the heavier crate; use the total last.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: translate two conditional charges into one system and solve it
questions.stem: A printer shop charges a setup fee of s dollars plus c dollars per page, and 10 pages cost 30 dollars while 25 pages cost 60 dollars. What is the value of s? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Subtracting the two bills removes the setup fee, so 15 pages cost 30 dollars and c equals 2 dollars per page. Then 10 pages cost 20, leaving s equal to 10 dollars from the first bill, and the check against the second is 10 plus 50 equal to 60. Reading the first bill alone as the setup fee, without removing the page charges, gives 30 instead.
questions.hint: Subtract one bill from the other to eliminate the fee, then solve for the page rate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: solve a system stated in standard form by eliminating after scaling
questions.stem: A system reads 2x plus 3y equal to 12 and 4x plus 5y equal to 23. Solving it, what is the value of x? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Doubling the first equation gives 4x plus 6y equal to 24, and subtracting the second equation leaves y equal to 1. Substituting back gives 2x equal to 9, so x equal to 4.5, and the second equation checks as 18 plus 5 equal to 23. Subtracting in the wrong order, or doubling the second equation instead of the first, are the routes to a wrong pair.
questions.hint: Scale the first equation so the x coefficients match, then subtract.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between an inconsistent and a consistent system
questions.stem: A teacher shows a class two solution grids for the same system: one grid is blank because the lines never meet, and the other has a single filled cell where the lines cross. Which statement about the two systems is correct?

options.text: The blank grid means no solution exists, and the filled cell gives the unique solution
The blank grid means the system has infinitely many solutions that are simply not drawn
options.misconception: believes an empty drawing proves an infinite solution set instead of an empty one

options.text: The filled cell is only an estimate, since a grid can never give an exact solution
options.misconception: assumes drawn points are always approximate and never check against an equation

options.text: Both systems are inconsistent, because grids cannot show where two equations agree
options.misconception: doubts the method entirely rather than reading what each grid displays

questions.explanation: The solutions of a system are the points shared by both lines, so when the lines are parallel nothing is shared and the solution set is empty. When the lines cross, exactly one point is shared, and that point satisfies both equations, so it is the unique solution. The grids record the same facts that the algebra produces, one blank and one filled.
questions.hint: A solution of a system is a point that both lines have in common.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: apply a system to a break-even situation in context
questions.stem: A van costs 2000 dollars to hire plus 0.4 dollars per kilometre with one firm, and 1200 dollars plus 0.9 dollars per kilometre with another. At what distance do the two charges become equal? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Setting the two costs equal gives 2000 plus 0.4d equal to 1200 plus 0.9d, so 800 equal to 0.5d and d equal to 1600 kilometres. The check is that 2000 plus 640 is 2640, matching 1200 plus 1440. Subtracting the smaller fixed charge from the larger but also reversing the per kilometre difference gives 0.5 in the wrong place, which flips the distance.
questions.hint: Put the two cost rules equal, then collect the fixed charges and the per kilometre terms separately.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a linear rule from a rule that graphs elsewhere
questions.stem: A student plots four rules and claims that any rule written with an x and a y makes a straight line. Which of the four plotted rules is a counterexample to that claim?

options.text: y equal to 3 times x, then plus 2, then multiplied by itself minus 5
y equal to 4x plus 1, which is a straight line
options.misconception: mistakes an ordinary slope-intercept rule for a counterexample to a true claim

options.text: y equal to 7, which has no x in it at all
options.misconception: believes a rule with no x term cannot be a line of its own

options.text: y equal to 12 minus 0.5x, which falls steadily
options.misconception: assumes a negative slope makes a rule stop being a straight line

questions.explanation: Only a rule whose output is a constant plus a constant times the input graphs as a straight line, and the first option squares its own value, so the output grows faster than any constant multiple of the input. The other three rules are all of the constant plus multiple form, including the one with no x, which is a horizontal line. The claimed rule of thumb holds only for that family of forms, so a multiplied or squared term breaks it.
questions.hint: Ask of each rule whether the output changes by the same amount each time the input steps by 1.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: read a table of a linear rule to find a missing output
questions.stem: A printer logs pages against cost, and the line passes through the points where pages are 0 and cost is 5, pages are 4 and cost is 17, and pages are 6 and cost is 25. What cost does the graph give for 10 pages? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Between pages 0 and 4 the cost rises by 12 dollars, so the rate is 3 dollars per page and the rule is 5 plus 3 times the pages. At 10 pages that gives 5 plus 30 equal to 45 dollars, and the intermediate point at 6 pages confirms the slope. Reading the cost from the nearest listed point, 25, without extending the line, is the usual slip.
questions.hint: Find the slope from two listed points, then evaluate the rule at 10 pages.
